specPoints.text: understand how vector quantities differ from scalar quantities
understand that force is a vector quantity

primer.text: Every measured quantity in this course belongs to one of two families. One family reports only 'how much'; the other also reports 'which way'. This note defines the two families, sorts the familiar pairs — distance and displacement, speed and velocity — and then shows why force itself sits in the second family.

lessons.title: Scalars, vectors and their paired quantities
lessons.opening: A scalar reports a size and nothing else; a vector reports a size plus a direction. The distinction looks small until you meet the paired quantities: distance against displacement, and the route a walker actually takes against the straight line home. This lesson fixes the definitions and the standard pairings.
keyPoints: A scalar carries a magnitude only, with no direction attached.
A vector carries both a magnitude and a direction.
Distance is the total length of the path travelled, regardless of direction, so it is a scalar.
Displacement is the straight-line separation of the finishing point from the starting point, including the direction, so it is a vector.
Mass, energy, volume, density, temperature and power are scalars; weight, force, acceleration and momentum are vectors.

low.restatement: Ask one question: does the quantity need a direction to be complete? If no, it is a scalar; if yes, it is a vector.
low.analogy: A shopping receipt gives amounts only — that is scalar-style data. Directions to a hidden treasure need steps with headings — vector-style data.
low.examPointer: Sort-the-list questions are common; memorise the two columns rather than re-deriving them in the exam.

medium.restatement: Distance and displacement disagree whenever the path bends: the path length accumulates every turn, while the displacement records only the net straight-line outcome with its heading.
medium.analogy: The odometer adds up every bend of a mountain road (distance); the map's ruler ignores the bends and draws one arrow start-to-finish (displacement).
medium.examPointer: A full lap of a track gives a large distance but zero displacement — a favourite one-mark discriminator.

check.stem: Which statement separates vector quantities from scalar quantities?

options.text: Scalars are measured with instruments; vectors are estimated
options.explanation: Both families are measured the same way; the difference is direction, not equipment.

options.text: Scalars can be negative; vectors cannot
options.explanation: Sign conventions exist in both families and prove nothing about direction.

options.text: Vectors carry a magnitude and a direction; scalars carry a magnitude only
options.explanation: This is the definition of record for the two families.

options.text: Scalars apply to solids; vectors apply to moving things
options.explanation: Neither family is restricted by the state of matter or by motion.

check.stem: A runner completes one full 400 m lap and stops where she started. Which row gives her distance and displacement?

options.text: 400 m and 400 m
options.explanation: The displacement is not the lap length; start and finish coincide.

options.text: Zero and 400 m
options.explanation: That swaps the two quantities.

options.text: 400 m and zero
options.explanation: The path length is 400 m; the straight-line start-to-finish separation is zero.

options.text: Zero and zero
options.explanation: The travelled path length is not zero.

check.stem: Which of these is a vector quantity?

options.text: Energy
options.explanation: Energy reports a size only.

options.text: Displacement
options.explanation: Displacement includes the direction, which makes it a vector.

options.text: Temperature
options.explanation: Temperature has no direction attached.

options.text: Density
options.explanation: Density reports mass per volume — no direction.

check.stem: From the standard pairing table, which scalar stands opposite velocity?

options.text: Speed
options.explanation: Speed is the magnitude-only partner of velocity.

options.text: Distance
options.explanation: Distance pairs with displacement.

options.text: Mass
options.explanation: Mass has no vector partner in the table.

options.text: Power
options.explanation: Power is a scalar with no pairing here.

check.stem: A learner's mass reads 70 kg on Earth and 70 kg in orbit, while the force pressing her into the seat changes. The explanation is:

options.text: Mass is a scalar and stays put; the seat force involves direction and can vary
options.explanation: Mass carries magnitude only, so location leaves it alone; the varying quantity is a vector force.

options.text: Both quantities are scalars, so both must change together
options.explanation: The 70 kg reading does not change; the premise fails.

options.text: Mass secretly depends on the planet while weight does not
options.explanation: That inverts the actual behaviour.

options.text: Instruments stop working in orbit
options.explanation: The instruments are fine; the physics explains the readings.

check.stem: State the difference between distance and displacement.
check.modelAnswer: Distance is the total path length travelled with no direction attached; displacement is the straight-line separation of the finishing point from the starting point, including that direction.

check.stem: Give the scalar partner of velocity and of displacement.
check.modelAnswer: Velocity pairs with speed, and displacement pairs with distance.

check.stem: Explain why a student's distance travelled to school can differ from its displacement.
check.modelAnswer: The route along roads twists and turns, so the path length accumulates every bend. The displacement ignores the route entirely: it is one straight line from home to school with its heading, so it is usually shorter than the distance.

check.stem: A hiker walks 3 km east, then 4 km north. State the distance walked and describe the displacement.
check.modelAnswer: The distance is the whole path length: 3 km + 4 km = 7 km. The displacement is the straight line from start to finish, 5 km long, pointing diagonally between the two legs.

lessons.title: Velocity and force as vectors
lessons.opening: The pairing idea now meets motion and force. Speed copies distance's magnitude-only habit; velocity inherits displacement's direction. Force behaves the same way, which is why force arrows are drawn with proportional lengths and stated headings. This lesson turns both statements into working rules.
keyPoints: Speed measures the distance covered per unit time regardless of direction, so it is a scalar.
Velocity measures the displacement per unit time with the direction included, so it is a vector.
An object can keep a constant speed while its velocity changes, because the heading is turning.
Force is a vector: it has a magnitude and acts along a stated direction.
Force arrows are drawn with length proportional to magnitude, in the force's direction, and labelled with the force's name.
Directions that are neither horizontal nor vertical are described by an angle from the horizontal or the vertical.

low.restatement: Velocity is speed with a heading; force is a push or pull with a heading. Arrows show both facts at once.
low.analogy: A delivery app pin shows distance only; the rider's arrow on the map shows where the van is heading — the vector view.
low.examPointer: Any describe-the-force answer should carry a size in newtons and a direction — one without the other is incomplete.

medium.restatement: Because velocity is displacement per time, a turning path changes the velocity even at fixed pace; because force is a vector, two equal-magnitude forces can cancel or combine depending on their directions.
medium.analogy: Two identical dogs pulling a post in opposite ways hold it still; the same two pulling the same way drag it off — magnitudes alone never tell the story.
medium.examPointer: For diagram marks: state the scale, keep lengths proportional (a 4 N arrow twice a 2 N arrow) and label every arrow.

check.stem: Which statement defines velocity by comparison with speed?

options.text: Velocity is speed with the direction of travel included
options.explanation: Velocity is displacement per time — speed plus heading.

options.text: Velocity is speed measured over a longer time
options.explanation: The time window changes nothing about the family.

options.text: Velocity is speed divided by distance
options.explanation: That combination is not a defined quantity here.

options.text: Velocity and speed are interchangeable names
options.explanation: They belong to different families — the whole point of the pairing.

check.stem: A force of 100 N acts at 40° above the horizontal. What role does the 40° play?

options.text: It fixes the arrow's length on the diagram
options.explanation: The magnitude fixes the length; the angle fixes the heading.

options.text: It specifies the direction of the force relative to the horizontal
options.explanation: Angles anchor a vector's direction to a reference line.

options.text: It converts the force into a scalar
options.explanation: Stating a direction keeps the quantity a vector.

options.text: It is decorative — the force is fully described by 100 N
options.explanation: Without the angle the description is incomplete; the direction is essential.

check.stem: Two 50 N forces act on a peg along the same line. What outcomes are possible?

options.text: Only a 50 N resultant, whatever the arrangement
options.explanation: The arrangement along the line decides the resultant.

options.text: Zero if they oppose, 100 N if they align
options.explanation: Opposite directions cancel; same direction adds — the along-a-line law.

options.text: Always 100 N because both are 50 N
options.explanation: Adding ignores the direction arrangement.

options.text: Always zero because they are equal
options.explanation: Equal forces cancel only when opposed.

check.stem: A diagram's scale says 1 cm stands for 20 N. A second arrow is drawn half as long as the 3 cm arrow that shows 60 N. What force does the shorter arrow show?

options.explanation: Half the length is half the magnitude, not double.

options.text: 60 N — length carries no meaning
options.explanation: Length is precisely what encodes the magnitude.
A quarter of the length would give 15 N, not a half.
Equal scale means length proportional to magnitude: half the arrow, 30 N.

check.stem: Weight, W, is the gravitational force on an object. Its vector nature means a full answer names:

options.text: Its size in newtons and its downward direction
options.explanation: Magnitude plus direction — the pull towards the planet's centre.

options.text: Its size in kilograms
options.explanation: Kilograms measure mass, not force.

options.text: Its direction only
options.explanation: The size is equally required.

options.text: Nothing more once the object is named
options.explanation: Naming the object does not describe the force.

check.stem: Define velocity in terms of displacement.
check.modelAnswer: Velocity gives the displacement covered in each unit of time, with the direction of travel included.

check.stem: State the two features of a force that a drawn arrow must show.
check.modelAnswer: Its length, proportional to the magnitude, and its direction, matching the force's line of action — with the arrow labelled.

check.stem: Explain why a number alone can never fully describe a force.
check.modelAnswer: A number reports only the size. A force also acts along a line in a particular direction, and two same-sized forces can act in opposite ways and produce entirely different outcomes, so the heading must be stated alongside the newtons.

check.stem: A diagram's scale says 1 cm stands for 20 N. State the force shown by a 3 cm arrow at 30° below the horizontal.
check.modelAnswer: The arrow's length gives 3 × 20 = 60 N, and its heading is 30° below the horizontal, so the force is 60 N directed 30° below the horizontal.

glossary.definition: A quantity that carries a magnitude only, with no direction attached.
A quantity that carries both a magnitude and a direction.
The straight-line separation of the finishing point from the starting point, including the direction.
The displacement travelled per unit time, with the direction of travel included.

workedExample.prompt: Suggest how a training officer should explain the difference between mass and weight to junior astronauts, using the definitions of scalars and vectors.
steps: Recall the definitions: a scalar has magnitude only, a vector has magnitude and direction.
Mass has magnitude only, so it is a scalar — its value does not depend on location.
Weight is a force, so it has magnitude and direction, making it a vector — its value varies with location in space.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Mass is a scalar (magnitude only, location-independent); weight is a vector force (magnitude and direction, location-dependent).
